fixes.explanation: I get why you'd think so, baker. More signs and wonders sounds like it should change a king's mind. But God tells Moses that Pharaoh will not listen, even as the signs and wonders multiply (Exodus 7:3-4). So the answer is false. God goes on to say, “Then I will lay My hand on Egypt…” (Exodus 7:4)

Rulers sounds grand, baker, like somebody handed them a crown. But God calls Canaan “…the land where they lived as foreigners.” (Exodus 6:4) That's how the verse describes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in that land. God also says He made His covenant with them to give them the land. I think that makes the promise even sweeter.

Battle is a good guess, baker, but it isn't what Moses says. He tells the LORD, “…I am unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) Speech is the word he uses about himself. I think he's thinking about Pharaoh, king of Egypt, since that's who the LORD sent him to.

Search is a fun guess, friend, but it isn't the word. God says, “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart…” (Exodus 7:3) Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and the verse says harden, not search. That's the word God uses, so we leave it right there.

problems.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
Calling Abraham, Isaac and Jacob the new folks in town adds that they were recent arrivals. The passage says they lived in Canaan as foreigners.

The explanation says Moses is not worried about battle and describes his trouble as opening his mouth. The text says he considers himself unskilled in speech; it does not establish those other claims.
The toast-and-helmet comparison mixes two unrelated actions, so the joke does not match the situation it is meant to illustrate.
The pocket-search and pat-down jokes apply a human action to what God might do to Pharaoh's heart. Comparisons must stay on the human side of the moment.
